p45.residues: Bean residue return or removal for these particular comparisons remains unverified.
p45.method: Yield-matched fertilizer equivalent from a fitted continuous sole-maize response curve.
p45.name: Nadar and Faught (1984), East African Agricultural and Forestry Journal
p45.design: Katumani trials with sole-crop rotations and intercrops. Fertilizer equivalence was inferred from a continuous-maize fertilizer response curve.

rows.season: Kimutwa following maize short rains 1988/89 and 1989/90. Masii following maize long rains 1988 and 1989.
rows.soil: Kimutwa sandy clay loam (dystric Nitisol). Masii sand (Acrisol).
rows.residues: Returned and removed bean-residue treatments. The assignment below follows p. 156, with inconsistent treatment labels elsewhere in the thesis.
rows.method: Fitted fertilizer-equivalent estimates from measured field grain yields.
rows.locator: p. 156 and Table 37a; abstract rounds the full spread to 1–56
rows.caveat: Treat the full spread as reported, with low confidence in the residue-by-season mapping. Page 147 assigns Kimutwa ranges of 14–24 to returned and 16–56 to removed residue and gives one Masii pair. The printed 1989/90 fits also conflict with part of p. 156.
rows.measure_label: Common bean · maize grain-yield fertilizer equivalent

rows.residues: RotNR removed bean residue. RotRR returned bean residue. Treatment codes from pp. 54–55.
rows.method: P49 calculation from the printed quadratic field-yield fits using the smaller nonnegative N root.
rows.caveat: Overlaps the same Chui field trial. This cross-check uses the printed intercepts and avoids counting the result as a second study. It cannot adjudicate every residue-by-season claim.
rows.measure_label: Common bean · maize grain-yield fertilizer equivalent

rows.site: Mulungu and South Kivu farms, DR Congo
rows.season: First rotation season. Table 13 covers maize seasons 2002A, 2002B and 2003A.
rows.soil: Volcanic-derived highland soils in the original trial preview. Plot-specific soil classes unavailable.
rows.residues: Residue handling unreported in the accessible author summary and table.
rows.method: Fertilizer replacement estimated from field yield response, reported by the original trial authors.
rows.caveat: Climbing-bean system in a highland environment. The full 2011 chapter remains unavailable and the endpoints cannot be assigned to individual residue treatments.
rows.measure_label: Common bean · maize grain-yield fertilizer equivalent

rows.season: Two cycles of short-rains legumes followed by long-rains maize. Calendar years unreported.
rows.soil: Sandy clay Rhodic Ferralsol, pH 5.6 and low total N and available P.
rows.residues: Grain harvested and aboveground residues returned, including pigeonpea litter. Rotation plots got P and no mineral N.
rows.method: Fitted fertilizer equivalents from measured maize grain yields and the continuous-maize urea response.
rows.caveat: Different grain legumes. Moisture stress around tasselling limited maize yield. The study reported no significant maize grain yield differences among the three legume rotations.
rows.measure_label: Other legumes · maize grain-yield fertilizer equivalent

rows.season: Rainy-season pigeonpea in 1979, harvested January 1980. Following maize in 1980 rains.
rows.soil: Black Vertisol, topsoil pH 8.3 and 0.03% total N.
rows.residues: Intact aboveground plant parts were removed at harvest. The authors discuss fallen leaves as a possible contribution.
rows.method: Estimated fertilizer N needed after each comparator to match the measured dry matter response of zero-N maize after sole pigeonpea.
rows.locator: Table 7 and results p. 137; Figure 3 p. 140
rows.caveat: Uses total aboveground dry matter as the matched response. The comparison is outside East Africa and uses a different legume.

rows.season: Beans in 2003 short rains, maize in 2004 long rains.
rows.soil: Fields stratified by high, medium and low fertility. Table 3 reports texture and 0–20 cm soil chemistry by zone and fertility group.
rows.residues: Harvested grain and returned remaining bean residues, incorporated about 15 cm deep. Maize planted 35–45 days later.
rows.method: Field residue N calculated from measured biomass and N concentration.
rows.caveat: Residue N is a mass applied before maize, including N that may remain unavailable to the maize.

rows.season: 2004 long-rains maize sowing after 2003 short-rains beans.
rows.soil: Top 0–15 cm, across the trial's fertility classes.
rows.residues: Sampled about 45 days after incorporating bean residues.
rows.method: Measured extractable mineral N, scaled with soil bulk density.
rows.caveat: These are soil N stocks at sowing. An attributable bean credit would require a matched change or control.
rows.measure_label: Soil mineral N stock at maize sowing

rows.season: 2014 short-rains legumes followed by 2014 long-rains maize, as labeled by the study.
rows.soil: Mean pH 6.2 in both districts, with mean topsoil clay of 500 and 390 g/kg, respectively.
rows.residues: Residues remained in the field. Maize received no direct nutrient addition. P, inoculum and manure were applied to the preceding legumes only.
rows.method: Field-measured differences in maize aboveground N uptake versus maize after the same unamended legumes. Published means across sites.
rows.locator: Table 6 and Nutrient uptake and production in maize

estimates.label: Bean with inoculant and 30 kg P/ha
Bean with inoculant, 30 kg P/ha and 10 t manure/ha
Soybean with inoculant and 30 kg P/ha
Soybean with inoculant, 30 kg P/ha and 10 t manure/ha

rows.caveat: The comparator is unamended bean or soybean, so the increases include residual effects of added inputs. Maize after soybean produced no grain at Bugesera, where its reported N uptake was stover only.

rows.crop: Pigeonpea and lablab, sole and with maize
rows.site: Riroda, Arri and Dareda, Babati, Tanzania
rows.season: 2017/18 and 2018/19 preceding systems, then unfertilized maize in 2019/20.
rows.soil: Three agroecological zones. Plot soil classes or textures are unreported in the sections checked.
rows.residues: Aboveground residues removed except fallen legume leaves.
rows.method: Differences from measured grain N means for continuous maize, using the control and P-only contrast in Table 6.
rows.caveat: Grain N uptake measures part of the successor's N demand. Two previous growing seasons and different legume species limit transfer to one bean season.

rows.season: Bimodal trial, November 1989–February 1996. Litter sampled from 1992 to 1994 long-rains seasons.
rows.residues: Cowpea haulms and pigeonpea stalks removed. Fallen foliage incorporated.
rows.method: Estimated annual nutrient return from measured fallen litter and nutrient concentration.
rows.caveat: The study reports 30 kg N/ha in the year of cowpea/pigeonpea cultivation, which recurred every second year. This is annual litter return into the soil, with subsequent availability unresolved.
rows.measure_label: Annual N returned through fallen litter

rows.soil: Dominant Ferralsols, mean pH 5.8 and mean clay 36.9%.
rows.residues: Aboveground biomass left to farmers. Retention was unmeasured.
rows.method: Difference in measured maize grain yield after climbing versus bush bean within each DAP treatment.
rows.caveat: The no-DAP contrast was nonsignificant. Both maize treatments received 46 kg N/ha as urea, with added N and P in DAP plots. Grain yield differences cannot resolve a fertilizer N credit.

limit: Fertilizer equivalence depends on the crop, soil, weather, residue management and maize response. It can include rotational effects unrelated to nitrogen. Field-level credit and rotation suitability at the Makueni coordinate remain unverified.
